newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: INTERVIEW - Tenaga chief detects rebound.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Tenaga chief detects rebound.

text.p: Tenaga Nasional Bhd's new chairman detects a rebound in confidence in Malaysia's state-controlled power utility, whose credibility has been jarred by blackouts and charges of inefficiency.

Ahmad Tajuddin Ali, 48, was appointed to head Tenaga in September to replace Ani Arope, whose contract was not renewed following the August 3 blackout that blanketed peninsula Malaysia for 12 to 15 hours.
"I think I'm getting positive indications that things are heading in the right direction," Tajuddin, a nuclear engineer, said in an interview late on Monday.
Tajuddin, who has previously said the utility must improve its management efficiency, was recruited from the Standards and Industrial Research Institute of Malaysia, where he was director-general.

He said the signs of better sentiment toward Tenaga include an improvement in its stock price. The shares, which hit a new year low after the August blackout, are now trading about 15 percent above that level. It closed at 9.80 ringgit on Monday.
Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's comments last week that Tenaga had to be protected from competition by independent power producers also showed a rebound in sentiment, Tajuddin said.
Mahathir, who sharply criticised Tenaga over the blackout, is scheduled to visit the utility's headquarters on Thursday for the first time since Tajuddin took over, Tenaga officials said.
Tenaga, which is 70 percent owned by the government, was also criticised for a 10-day outage on Penang island in June 1995. The northern state is the hub of the country's electronics industry.
Tenaga's bonds were downgraded by at least one U.S. rating agency after the blackout this year, leading analysts to worry about its financing in the future.
A British consultancy firm has been hired to look into Tenaga's operations.
But Tajuddin said his meetings with Hong Kong fixed income investors recently and a conference with energy analysts in Kuala Lumpur last week were helping to restore faith.
Tenaga has said it will spend about four billion ringgit ($1.6 billion) in 1997 for capital expenditures, and will probably raise $1 billion in international capital markets.
"We'll probably go out next year (to raise it) when the time is right," Tajuddin said. "Indications are that we shouldn't have any problem, even if we want it tomorrow."
But Tajuddin said he was still treading carefully.
While Tenaga had been expected to ask for a rate hike this year, Tajuddin said he would not propose one until the company could prove it could deliver power "efficiently and reliably".
Asked if he balked at being offered the closely scrutinised Tenaga post, Tajuddin said: "No, I take it in my stride."
"I still have a smile at the end of the day, and I try to get support from within first and also from outside," he said.
